cables.excerpt: Two years before the civil war: Fatah members arrested at Beirut airport with 10 kg of TNT. Black September threatened to blow up the airport. A 2-kg bomb was found and defused. The Lebanese Army G-2 assessed that Arafat may have covertly tipped off Lebanese authorities about a bomb planted by his own movement’s hardliners he could not control.
cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review, 30 June 2005 · Now UNCLASSIFIED

Summary
Following several weekend incidents involving fedayeen[1] that produced considerable tension here, Lebanese authorities have instituted heavy security precautions in and around Beirut Airport. The Lebanese Army’s patrolling activities along the Israeli border have also been intensified. We regard these developments as encouraging initial signs on the part of the new Lebanese government.

1.
Beirut International Airport is under strict security on April 30, following a weekend of tension that began the afternoon of April 27 when airport authorities — in the process of conducting a thorough search of departing passengers — arrested three men (2 Lebanese and 1 Palestinian) who were about to board an Air France flight to Paris with 10 kilograms of TNT and detonating devices in their baggage.[2] Upon learning that the individuals were Fatah[3] members, Lebanese Army and security forces — fearing an adverse fedayeen reaction when the arrests became known — moved quickly to block the main access road to the airport and cordon off the southern entrance to the Sabra quarter and the fedayeen stronghold at the nearby Shatila refugee camp.[4]

No reaction occurred that day, but on April 28 airport authorities received a series of anonymous telephone calls threatening that BSO[5] would blow up airport facilities if the arrested fedayeen and their munitions were not released. One such call, made late on April 28, indicated that a bomb had been placed in a water cooler at the airport terminal. A hectic search of the building — supervised personally by Minister of Interior Bashir al-Awar[6] and senior Lebanese security officials — led to the discovery of a 2-kilogram plastic charge timed to explode at 2:30 AM on April 29 in a water cooler.

2.
As of noon on April 30, army and security forces are maintaining intensified security precautions around the entire airport area, with roadblocks established on main access routes, cars being thoroughly searched, and only travelers being allowed to enter the terminal proper. Airline traffic continues as scheduled. The general atmosphere of tension was heightened further on the night of April 28–29 by the explosion of a stick of dynamite thrown at the Jordanian ambassador’s residence from a passing car (no casualties resulted and damage was negligible).

3.
Minister of Interior Awar has stated publicly that the GOL resolved not to give in to blackmail in connection with the April 27 airport incident. We understand from a reliable Presidency source that Awar received orders directly from President Frangieh[7] himself not to yield to the bomb threat.

The Lebanese Army investigation is still in progress, but G-2 believes that the airport bomb was planted by BSO activists acting in defiance of Arafat’s desire to avoid confrontation with the GOL over the April 27 arrests — and that the phone call which led to the bomb’s discovery was possibly an effort by Arafat to assist Lebanese authorities in warding off action by BSO hotheads whose behavior he could not control.[8]

4.
In addition to the GOL’s firmness with the fedayeen over the airport affair, both Lebanese Army and UNTSO[9] sources report that the Lebanese Army has intensified its patrolling in the frontier area over the weekend of April 28–29, with patrols more frequent by night and day.

5. Comment
Although we are unable to say how far the tightening of GOL security precautions will go or how long it will continue — especially if it results in armed clashes between the army and reckless fedayeen elements — we regard it as a heartening initial sign of determination on the part of a new government that has yet to receive a parliamentary vote of confidence.[10]

HOUGHTON[11]

SUBJECT: INTERNAL SECURITY DEVELOPMENTS IN LEBANON

SUMMARY: FOLLOWING SEVERAL WEEKEND INCIDENTS INVOLVING FEDAYEEN THAT PRODUCED CONSIDERABLE TENSION HERE, LEBANESE AUTHORITIES HAVE INSTITUTED HEAVY SECURITY PRECAUTIONS IN AND AROUND BEIRUT AIRPORT. LEBANESE ARMY'S PATROLLING ACTIVITIES ALONG ISRAELI BORDER HAVE ALSO BEEN INTENSIFIED. WE REGARD THESE DEVELOPMENTS AS ENCOURAGING INITIAL SIGNS ON PART OF NEW LEBANESE GOVT. END SUMMARY.

1. BEIRUT INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT UNDER STRICT SECURITY APR 30 AFTER WEEKEND OF TENSION THAT BEGAN AFTERNOON APR 27, WHEN AIRPORT AUTHORITIES -- IN PROCESS OF CONDUCTING THOROUGH SEARCH OF DEPARTING PASSENGERS -- ARRESTED 3 MEN (2 LEBANESE AND 1 PALESTINIAN) WHO WERE ABOUT TO BOARD AIR FRANCE FLIGHT TO PARIS WITH 10 KGS OF TNT AND DETONATING DEVICES IN THEIR BAGGAGE. UPON LEARNING THAT CULPRITS WERE FATAH MEMBERS, LEBANESE ARMY AND SECURITY FORCES -- FEARING ADVERSE FEDAYEEN REACTION WHEN ARRESTS BECAME KNOWN -- MOVED QUICKLY TO BLOCK MAIN ACCESS ROAD TO AIRPORT AND CORDON OFF SOUTHERN ENTRANCE TO SABRA QUARTER AND FEDAYEEN STRONGHOLD AT NEARBY SHATILA REFUGEE CAMP. NO REACTION OCCURRED THAT DAY, BUT ON APR 28 AIRPORT AUTHORITIES RECEIVED SERIES OF ANONYMOUS TELEPHONE CALLS THREATENING THAT BSO WOULD BLOW UP AIRPORT FACILITIES IF ARRESTED FEDAYEEN AND THEIR MUNITIONS WERE NOT RELEASED. ONE SUCH CALL, MADE LATE APR 28, ACTUALLY INDICATED BOMB HAD BEEN PLACED IN WATER-COOLER AT AIRPORT TERMINAL, AND HECTIC SEARCH OF BUILDING, SUPERVISED PERSONALLY BY MININT BASHIR AL AWAR AND SENIOR LEBANESE SECURITY OFFICIALS, LED TO DISCOVERY OF 2-KG PLASTIC CHARGE TIMED TO EXPLODE AT 0230 HOURS APR 29 IN A WATER COOLER.

2. AS OF NOON APR 30, ARMY AND SECURITY FORCES ARE MAINTAINING INTENSIFIED SECURITY PRECAUTIONS AROUND ENTIRE AIRPORT AREA, WITH ROADBLOCKS ESTABLISHED ON MAIN ACCESS ROUTES, CARS BEING THOROUGHLY SEARCHED, AND ONLY TRAVELLERS BEING ALLOWED TO ENTER TERMINAL PROPER. AIRLINE TRAFFIC CONTINUES AS SCHEDULED. GENERAL ATMOSPHERE OF TENSION, HOWEVER, WAS HEIGHTENED FURTHER NIGHT OF APR 28-29 BY EXPLOSION OF STICK OF DYNAMITE THROWN AT JORDANIAN AMBASSADOR'S RESIDENCE FROM PASSING CAR (NO CASUALTIES RESULTED AND DAMAGE WAS NEGLIGIBLE), AND STRICTER SECURITY MEASURES HAVE BEEN ESTABLISHED IN THAT NEIGHBORHOOD AS WELL.

3. MININT AWAR HAS STATED PUBLICLY THAT GOL HAD RESOLVED NOT TO GIVE IN TO BLACKMAIL IN CONNECTION WITH APR 27 AIRPORT INCIDENT. (WE UNDERSTAND FROM RELIABLE PRESIDENCY SOURCE THAT AWAR RECEIVED ORDERS DIRECTLY FROM PRES FRANGIE HIMSELF NOT TO GIVE IN TO BOMB THREAT.) LEBANESE ARMY INVESTIGATION OF ENTIRE AFFAIR STILL IN PROGRESS, BUT G-2 BELIEVES THAT AIRPORT BOMB WAS PLANTED BY BSO ACTIVISTS ACTING IN DEFIANCE OF ARAFAT'S DESIRE TO AVOID CONFRONTATION WITH GOL OVER APR 27 ARRESTS AND THAT PHONE CALL WHICH LED TO BOMB'S DISCOVERY WAS POSSIBLY EFFORT BY ARAFAT TO ASSIST LEBANESE AUTHORITIES WARD OFF ACTION BY BSO HOT HEADS WHOSE BEHAVIOR HE COULD NOT CONTROL (DETAILS BEING REPORTED VIA SEPARATE CHANNEL).

4. IN ADDITION TO GOL FIRMNESS WITH FEDAYEEN RE AIRPORT AFFAIR, WE HAVE BEEN TOLD BY BOTH LEBANESE ARMY AND UNTSO SOURCES THAT LEBANESE ARMY HAS INTENSIFIED ITS PATROLLING IN FRONTIER AREA OVER WEEKEND APR 28-29. PATROLS MORE FREQUENT BY NIGHT AND DAY.

5. COMMENT: ALTHOUGH WE UNABLE SAY HOW FAR TIGHTENING UP OF GOL SECURITY PRECAUTIONS DESCRIBED ABOVE WILL GO OR HOW LONG IT WILL CONTINUE -- ESPECIALLY IF IT RESULTS IN ARMED CLASHES BETWEEN ARMY AND RECKLESS FEDAYEEN ELEMENTS -- WE REGARD IT AS HEARTENING INITIAL SIGN OF DETERMINATION ON PART OF NEW GOVT THAT HAS YET TO RECEIVE PARLIAMENTARY VOTE OF CONFIDENCE.

HOUGHTON

footnotes: Fedayeen (Arabic: فدائيين, “those who sacrifice themselves”): Palestinian armed fighters. In the Lebanese context of 1973, “fedayeen” referred collectively to the armed members of PLO constituent organizations — Fatah, PFLP, DFLP, and others — operating from bases in Lebanese refugee camps under the protection of the 1969 Cairo Agreement.

10 kilograms of TNT with detonating devices constitutes a significant quantity of high explosive capable of catastrophic damage to an aircraft or airport facility. The three individuals — two Lebanese and one Palestinian — were about to board a civilian Air France flight to Paris. This event — a Fatah-linked bomb plot targeting civilian aviation departing from Lebanese soil — is documented in this cable, filed April 30, 1973. It does not appear in the standard historical account of pre-war Lebanon.

Fatah (حركة التحرير الوطني الفلسطيني, Palestinian National Liberation Movement): The largest constituent faction of the PLO, founded in 1959 by Yasser Arafat and others. Fatah was the dominant organization within the PLO and operated the largest armed presence in Lebanon under the Cairo Agreement. The fact that the arrested individuals were identified as Fatah members — not a smaller splinter group — made the incident politically sensitive for Arafat’s leadership of the PLO.

Shatila refugee camp: Palestinian refugee camp established in 1949 on the southwestern outskirts of Beirut. By 1973, Shatila and the adjacent Sabra area had become a significant armed base for Palestinian factions. The Lebanese Army’s immediate cordon of the camp upon the April 27 arrests — anticipating a violent response — documents the Lebanese state’s awareness of the armed capacity in the camps and its own vulnerability to retaliation. The same Shatila camp would be the site of the September 1982 massacre.

BSO: Black September Organization. A covert Fatah-linked terrorist unit established in the aftermath of the 1970–71 Jordanian Army’s expulsion of Palestinian armed groups (“Black September”). The BSO was responsible for the September 1972 Munich Olympics massacre in which 11 Israeli athletes and coaches were killed. By 1973, BSO was active in international terrorism while Arafat maintained official distance from its operations. The BSO’s threat to blow up Beirut International Airport — and its actual planting of a bomb in the airport terminal — is documented in this cable.

Bashir al-Awar: Lebanese Minister of Interior in the cabinet of Prime Minister Amin al-Hafez, formed in April 1973. His personal supervision of the search that discovered the airport bomb documents the seriousness with which the Lebanese government treated the threat. This is the same new government the cable refers to as not yet having received a parliamentary vote of confidence.

President Suleiman Frangieh (1910–1992): President of Lebanon 1970–1976. His direct order to the Interior Minister not to yield to the BSO bomb threat — received from a reliable Presidency source by the Embassy — is documented in this cable. This is the same Frangieh who would be hospitalized during the April 13, 1975 crisis (cable 1975BEIRUT04749) and who would personally handle contacts with Kataeb leader Gemayel during the ceasefire negotiations (cable 1975BEIRUT04860). The 1973 cable establishes his governing pattern: direct engagement and a firm stance toward Palestinian armed pressure — a stance that would become harder to maintain as the 1970s progressed.

This paragraph contains one of the most significant intelligence assessments in the pre-war cable record. The Lebanese Army G-2 believed: (a) the bomb was planted by BSO activists acting against Arafat’s wishes; and (b) the anonymous phone call that led to the bomb’s discovery was possibly Arafat himself covertly assisting Lebanese authorities against his own organization’s hardliners. If the G-2 assessment was accurate, it documents an internal PLO command structure problem in 1973 that is directly continuous with the internal disputes documented in the 1975 cables (cable 1975BEIRUT04860 records an unconfirmed report of a similar Arafat-vs-subordinates dispute during the April 1975 ceasefire negotiations). This assessment is in the diplomatic record as of April 30, 1973. It has not been cited in the standard historical account of PLO operations in Lebanon.

UNTSO: United Nations Truce Supervision Organization. The UN observer mission established in 1948 to monitor the Israel-Arab armistice agreements. UNTSO observers stationed along the Lebanese-Israeli border provided the U.S. Embassy with an independent source for reports on Lebanese Army patrol activity — distinct from Lebanese Army self-reporting.

The cable’s framing of this as the behavior of a “new government” — one that had not yet received a parliamentary vote of confidence — contextualizes the firmness as a deliberate political choice by a government trying to establish its credibility. The Hafez cabinet had been appointed in April 1973 amid a political crisis triggered by Israeli commando raids into Beirut. The government’s willingness to confront the BSO despite its fragile political position is documented here.

Dwight J. Houghton: U.S. Ambassador to Lebanon 1970–1974. Houghton’s posting preceded that of G. McMurtrie Godley (1974–1976), whose cables document the April 1975 crisis. Houghton’s 1973 reporting on PLO behavior and Lebanese government responses provides the pre-war context for understanding the structural conditions that produced the 1975 crisis. His characterization of Lebanese government firmness as “heartening” would prove, in retrospect, to have been reporting on a pattern that the Lebanese state was progressively losing the capacity to sustain.

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
Two years before the war

On the afternoon of April 27, 1973, airport security at Beirut International Airport found something extraordinary in the baggage of three men about to board an Air France flight to Paris: 10 kilograms of TNT and the devices to detonate it. The men were Fatah members.

What happened over the following 48 hours is documented in this cable, filed by the U.S. Embassy on April 30, 1973. It does not appear in the standard historical account of pre-war Lebanon.

The bomb threat and the bomb that was found

When news of the arrests spread, the Lebanese Army immediately cordoned Shatila refugee camp — a documented acknowledgment that it expected armed retaliation from the camp’s armed organizations. The next day, the Black September Organization called the airport and threatened to blow up its facilities if the arrested men and their explosives were not released.

One call went further: a bomb had been placed in an airport water cooler. The Lebanese Minister of Interior personally supervised the search. They found it: a 2-kilogram plastic charge, timed to explode at 2:30 AM on April 29.

The G-2 assessment: what it means

The Lebanese Army’s military intelligence branch — G-2 — offered a conclusion that is among the most significant in the pre-war diplomatic record. The airport bomb, G-2 assessed, was planted by BSO hardliners acting against Arafat’s explicit wishes. Arafat had been trying to avoid a confrontation with the Lebanese government. And the anonymous phone call that led to the bomb’s discovery was, G-2 believed, possibly Arafat himself — covertly helping Lebanese authorities defuse an action by his own organization’s elements he could not control.

This conclusion — in the Lebanese Army’s intelligence assessment, transmitted through the U.S. Embassy, on record at the State Department as of April 30, 1973 — documents a specific dynamic: Arafat leading an organization with armed factions he could not fully command. Read alongside the 1975 cables, which document a strikingly similar internal PLO command dispute during the April ceasefire negotiations, the pattern spans two years and is consistent.

Frangieh said no

President Suleiman Frangieh gave a direct order to his Interior Minister: do not yield to the blackmail. The Embassy understood this from a reliable Presidency source. The new Lebanese government — which had not yet received a parliamentary vote of confidence — stood firm.

The Embassy called this a “heartening initial sign of determination.” Two years later, during the April 13 crisis, Frangieh would be in the hospital recovering from surgery, the Lebanese Army would have orders to stand aside, and the “determination” the Embassy saw in 1973 would be very difficult to find.

What this cable establishes

The standard historical account of the Lebanese Civil War begins, in most treatments, with April 13, 1975. This cable establishes that the structural conditions of that war — PLO armed factions operating autonomously from Lebanese soil, the Lebanese state attempting to enforce order and being met with armed blackmail, Arafat’s imperfect control over hardline elements within his own movement — were documented realities two full years earlier.

The war did not begin on April 13, 1975. The diplomatic record shows it had been building, documented in real time, since at least 1973.

cables.excerpt: More than two years before the civil war: the Lebanese Army deploys aircraft and tanks against Palestinian refugee camps in Beirut. The Prime Minister resigns before dawn. The U.S. Embassy documents Syrian manipulation of Palestinian hardliners to torpedo negotiations, and records Arafat in diplomatic meetings when his own movement's factions opened fire.

Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review · Now UNCLASSIFIED

1.
As of 0700Z [7:00 AM Greenwich Mean Time, May 8], the Beirut area is calm after the Lebanese Army had expended considerable firepower — including aircraft and tank fire[1] — against targets in and around refugee camps in the general southeastern quadrant of Beirut: specifically Sabra/Chatila, Bir Hassan, and Borj el Brajne camps.[2] The rest of the country has thus far remained calm despite the fighting in Beirut, although army units in the South Bekaa are fully alert to possible infiltration from Syria.[3]

2.
At 0500Z [5:00 AM GMT], Prime Minister Hafez resigned,[4] and the cabinet went into session to examine next steps — most important of which could be the designation of a military man as interim Prime Minister.

3.
The fighting which broke out at about 1900Z [7:00 PM GMT] on May 7 appears, in the light of day, to have been a deliberate attempt by some fedayeen elements to torpedo any possibility of stabilizing fedayeen–GOL relations on a new basis.[5] Army G-2 believes that the PDFLP and PFLP/GC[6] were involved, with probably some elements of PFLP and possibly Sa’iqa[7] as well. There are also reports of involvement by armed elements from the LCP.[8]

Between 1900Z and 1930Z, there was widespread firing of rockets and mortars, directed at two or three military installations and the airport but also at random throughout the city. At the same time, several cars full of armed men drove through parts of the city firing at police and other targets. The obvious design was to create panic and touch off a major army–fedayeen confrontation.

4.
At the time the fighting began,[9] Arafat[10] was meeting with several Lebanese political figures — including Saeb Salam[11] and Raymond Edde[12] — to discuss the progress of talks with the GOL on May 7. In these talks — in which Egyptian and Syrian representatives were present — Prime Minister Hafez had reached “some sort of vague first-step agreement” on the route to obtaining a new understanding. According to army participants in the talks, this agreement was nowhere near as detailed or firm — or as pro-fedayeen — as announced by the Syrian Foreign Minister[13] upon his return to Damascus. This is merely one of the reasons for GOL suspicion that a Syrian hand was working behind the scene.[14]

5.
Developments in the immediate future will depend on such factors as: whether Arafat will try and be able to calm the bulk of Fatah fedayeen, keeping as many as possible out of the fighting; whether leftist Lebanese elements (LCP, Ba’ath, PPS, etc.) and Sunni Muslims generally join the fedayeen in continuing the fight with the GOL; and whether the GOL decides actually to move into the camps — which it has not yet done.

Morale of the army continues to be good, with no sign of Muslim/Christian dissension.[15] Reinforcements have been brought into the Beirut area from the south. Army controls around the camps and checkpoints elsewhere are much tighter than before. The atmosphere in Beirut is very tense, with a curfew reimposed and the army — in accordance with the state of emergency — in charge of all security. Emergency law is being used to impose strict censorship on the press and also authorizes the army to arrest virtually anyone suspected of creating trouble. No American casualties reported and no Americans known to be in danger. Embassy well protected. Americans, especially tourists, are quite nervous. We are advising everyone to stay put. Airport closed.

6.
At 0800Z, an EMBOFF talked to the army (Kanaan[16]), who informed us that Arafat is — RPT — is trying to calm his troops. Immediately thereafter, Tony Frangie[17] told us that a new ceasefire came into effect as of 0800Z, and that it is quite possible that the Prime Minister will once again withdraw his resignation.

Tony confirmed that the GOL intends to take a tough line with the fedayeen in any talks and will not give in to demands, reach any sort of formal agreement, or accept the sort of nonsense that Khaddam[18] announced in Damascus has been agreed upon on May 8.[19]

HOUGHTON[20]

WITH GOL ON MAY 7. IN THESE TALKS (IN WHICH EGYPTIAN AND SYRIAN REPS WERE
PRESENT) PRIME MINISTER HAFEZ HAD REACHED SOME SORT OF VAGUE FIRST-STEP
AGREEMENT ON ROUTE TO OBTAINING NEW UNDERSTANDING. ACCORDING TO ARMY
PARTICIPANTS IN TALKS, THIS AGREEMENT NOWHERE NEAR AS DETAILED OR FIRM (OR AS
PRO-FEDAYEEN) AS ANNOUNCED BY SYRIAN FOREIGN MINISTER UPON HIS RETURN TO
DAMASCUS. (THIS IS MERELY ONE OF REASONS FOR GOL SUSPICION THAT SYRIAN HAND
WORKING BEHIND SCENE.)

5. DEVELOPMENTS FOR IMMEDIATE FUTURE WILL DEPEND ON SUCH FACTORS AS WHETHER OR
NOT ARAFAT WILL TRY AND BE ABLE TO CALM BULK OF FATAH FEDAYEEN, KEEPING AS
MANY AS POSSIBLE OUT OF FIGHTING; WHETHER OR NOT LEFTIST LEBANESE ELEMENTS
(LCP, BAATH, PPS, ETC.) AND SUNNI MOSLEMS GENERALLY JOIN FEDAYEEN IN
CONTINUING FIGHT WITH GOL; AND WHETHER OR NOT GOL DECIDES ACTUALLY MOVE INTO
CAMPS (WHICH IT HAS NOT YET DONE). MORALE OF ARMY CONTINUES TO BE GOOD WITH
NO SIGN OF MOSLEM/CHRISTIAN DISSENSION. REINFORCEMENTS HAVE BEEN BROUGHT INTO
BEIRUT AREA FROM SOUTH. ARMY CONTROLS AROUND CAMPS AND CHECKPOINTS ELSEWHERE
MUCH TIGHTER THAN BEFORE. ATMOSPHERE IN BEIRUT IS VERY TENSE WITH CURFEW
REIMPOSED AND ARMY, IN ACCORDANCE STATE OF EMERGENCY, IN CHARGE OF ALL
SECURITY. EMERGENCY LAW BEING USED TO IMPOSE STRICT CENSORSHIP ON PRESS AND
ALSO AUTHORIZES ARMY ARREST VIRTUALLY ANYONE WHO SUSPECTED OF CREATING TROUBLE.
NO AMERICAN CASUALTIES REPORTED AND NO AMERICANS KNOWN TO BE IN DANGER. EMBASSY
WELL PROTECTED. AMERICANS, ESPECIALLY TOURIESTS, ARE QUITE NERVOUS. WE ADVISING
EVERYONE TO STAY PUT. AIRPORT CLOSED.

6. AT 0800Z EMBOFF TALKED TO ARMY (KANAAN) WHO INFORMS US THAT ARAFAT IS RPT IS
TRYING TO CALM HIS TROOPS. IMMEDIATELY THEREAFTER TONY FRANGIE TOLD US THAT NEW
CEASE-FIRE HAS COME INTO EFFECT AS OF 0800Z AND IT QUITE POSSIBLE THAT PRIME
MINISTER WILL ONCE AGAIN WITHDRAW HIS RESIGNATION. TONY CONFIRMED THAT GOL
INTENDS TAKE TOUGH LINE WITH FEDAYEEN IN ANY TALKS AND WILL NOT GIVE IN TO
DEMANDS, REACH ANY SORT OF FORMAL AGREEMENT, OR ACCEPT SORT OF NONESENSE THAT
KHADDAM ANNOUNCED IN DAMASCUS HAS BEEN AGREED UPON MAY 8.

HOUGHTON

footnotes: The cable reads "TAK FIRE" — an apparent teletype transmission error or abbreviation for "TANK FIRE." The corrected reading is supported by context: the cable describes the Lebanese Army employing aviation and armor in combined-arms operations against urban refugee camp targets. Such errors were common in teletype cable transmission of the era and are preserved verbatim in the raw text.

The Lebanese Army's use of aircraft and tank fire against Sabra/Chatila, Bir Hassan, and Borj el Brajne — three Palestinian refugee camps located in the heavily populated southeastern suburbs of Beirut — is one of the most significant facts in this cable. By the morning of May 8, 1973, the Lebanese state had committed its air force and armor against civilian-adjacent camps on Lebanese sovereign territory. This level of military force against Palestinian positions in Beirut had not previously occurred since the Lebanese Army was effectively prohibited from full enforcement by the 1969 Cairo Agreement. The cable reports this as already completed as of 0700Z — the fighting, and the army's response to it, had occurred overnight.

"Army units in South Bekaa fully alert to possible infiltration from Syria": the cable explicitly flags Syria as a potential external source of infiltration in the event of escalation. This concern is elaborated in paragraph 4, where the Embassy records GOL suspicion of a "Syrian hand working behind the scene." The South Bekaa — the Bekaa Valley's southern portion — shares a long border with Syria and was a known route for Palestinian and Syrian-backed armed movements into Lebanon.

Amin al-Hafez (1911–1989): Lebanese Sunni Muslim politician, Prime Minister of Lebanon from April 1973. His cabinet had been attempting to negotiate a revised agreement governing Palestinian armed activity in Lebanon when the May 7 fighting erupted. His resignation at 0500Z on May 8 — in the middle of an active military crisis — represented the collapse of civilian political authority at the moment it was most needed. As paragraph 6 records, he later withdrew the resignation. Al-Hafez should not be confused with Hafez al-Assad, the Syrian President at the time.

The Embassy's assessment that the May 7 fighting was a "deliberate attempt by some fedayeen elements to torpedo any possibility of stabilizing fedayeen-GOL relations" is a significant analytical judgment. It indicates that the Embassy did not regard the outbreak of fighting as accidental, reactive, or attributable to Lebanese Army provocation — but as a purposeful act by specific Palestinian factions intent on preventing a negotiated settlement. This assessment is filed at 0808Z on May 8, within hours of the events described.

PFLP/GC: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine — General Command. A breakaway faction from the PFLP founded in 1968 by Ahmad Jibril, a former Syrian Army officer. The PFLP/GC split from the PFLP over the latter's ideological emphasis, preferring purely military operations. Operating with close ties to Syrian intelligence and the Syrian military, the PFLP/GC was one of the Palestinian factions most resistant to accommodation with the Lebanese state and most susceptible to direction from Damascus. Its named involvement in the May 7 fighting — alongside the PDFLP and possibly Sa'iqa — is consistent with the cable's concurrent suspicion of Syrian manipulation of events.

Sa'iqa (formally "Vanguards of the Popular Liberation War" — Arabic: طلائع حرب التحرير الشعبية): Syrian Ba'ath Party-sponsored Palestinian armed faction operating in Lebanon. Unlike Fatah, which sought autonomy from Arab state influence, Sa'iqa was effectively an instrument of Syrian policy — its leadership appointed by Damascus and its operations coordinated with Syrian intelligence. Its possible involvement in the May 7 fighting — alongside the PFLP/GC, another Syrian-aligned faction — is one of the facts that generated GOL suspicion of a "Syrian hand working behind the scene," as the cable notes in paragraph 4.

LCP: Lebanese Communist Party (الحزب الشيوعي اللبناني). Founded in 1924, the LCP was a multi-sectarian Marxist party that aligned with the PLO and Palestinian resistance during the 1970s. The cable reports "armed elements" from the LCP as involved in the May 7 fighting — meaning that the confrontation was not exclusively Palestinian, but included Lebanese leftist factions. This is consistent with the pre-civil war pattern in which Palestinian armed organizations and Lebanese leftist parties increasingly coordinated against the Lebanese Army and the Maronite-dominated state.

The cable reads "AT TIME FIRMING BEGAN" — an apparent teletype transmission error for "AT TIME FIGHTING BEGAN." The corrected reading is unambiguous from context: the preceding paragraph describes the outbreak of fighting at 1900Z on May 7, and the subsequent sentence describes Arafat's activities during that fighting. The original error is preserved verbatim in the raw cable text.

Yasser Arafat (1929–2004): Chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organization and leader of Fatah. The cable's description of Arafat meeting with Lebanese political figures — including representatives of both communities — at the precise moment fighting broke out is significant. It places Arafat in a negotiating posture while other Palestinian factions (PDFLP, PFLP/GC, Sa'iqa) initiated military action. Whether Arafat had foreknowledge of the May 7 attacks and was using the negotiations as cover, or was genuinely caught off-guard by factions operating outside his control, is not resolved in this cable — though paragraph 6 reports he was "trying to calm his troops" by 0800Z.

Saeb Salam (1905–2000): Sunni Muslim politician from one of Beirut's most prominent families, a former Prime Minister of Lebanon (1952–1953, 1960–1961, 1970–1973). Salam had recently resigned as Prime Minister in April 1973, just days before the events documented in this cable, specifically over the question of the Lebanese Army's response to Palestinian armed activity — arguing the army was not doing enough. His presence in the negotiations documented in this cable, sitting alongside Arafat when fighting erupted, places a major Lebanese Sunni political figure in direct diplomatic contact with PLO leadership during the crisis.

Raymond Edde (1913–2000): Maronite Christian politician, leader of the National Bloc (Kataeb rival), and a consistently independent voice in Lebanese politics known for his opposition to Syrian influence and his criticism of both PLO armed activity in Lebanon and excessive Maronite intransigence. His presence in the negotiations alongside Arafat and Salam indicates that the talks involved cross-sectarian Lebanese political representation. Edde would later go into voluntary exile in Paris in 1976, citing threats to his life.

The "Syrian Foreign Minister" referred to is Abdul Halim Khaddam (1932–2020), Syrian Ba'ath politician who served as Foreign Minister 1970–1984 before becoming Vice President of Syria. A key operative of the Assad regime's Lebanon policy, Khaddam was closely involved in Syrian manipulation of Lebanese affairs throughout the civil war. The cable's note that Khaddam publicly announced terms in Damascus far more favorable to the fedayeen than what had actually been agreed — and that GOL army participants in the talks confirmed this discrepancy — is a specific documented instance of Syrian disinformation in the context of Lebanese-Palestinian negotiations.

"Syrian hand working behind the scene": the cable records this as GOL's own assessment, not merely Embassy speculation. The simultaneous involvement of PFLP/GC and Sa'iqa — both Syrian-aligned or Syrian-directed factions — in the May 7 fighting, combined with Khaddam's inflation of the agreement terms, constituted a coherent pattern: Syrian interest in preventing a stable Lebanese-Palestinian accommodation that might reduce Syrian leverage over both parties. This cable, filed May 8, 1973, documents U.S. Embassy awareness of Syrian manipulation of Lebanese-Palestinian relations more than two years before the civil war began.

"No sign of Muslim/Christian dissension" within the Lebanese Army: the cable explicitly notes the army's internal cohesion as of May 8, 1973. This cohesion would progressively erode over the following two years as the sectarian polarization of Lebanese society deepened. By early 1976, significant portions of the Lebanese Army — predominantly Muslim officers and enlisted men — mutinied and joined the Palestinian-LNM alliance, fracturing the institution entirely and removing the last restraint on full-scale civil war.

"Kanaan": the Lebanese Army contact referenced here has not been definitively identified. The name may refer to a senior Lebanese Army officer serving in a liaison capacity with the U.S. Embassy. It should not be confused with Ghazi Kanaan (1942–2005), the Syrian intelligence chief who would later dominate Lebanon — though that Syrian officer would not have had this role in 1973.

Tony Frangie (Toni Frangieh, 1942–1978): eldest son of President Suleiman Frangieh, serving at this time as a presidential aide and informal channel between the Lebanese Presidency and the U.S. Embassy. Tony Frangieh was the father of Suleiman Frangieh Jr., the current Lebanese political leader. He was assassinated on June 13, 1978, along with his wife, daughter, and bodyguards, in a pre-dawn raid on his home at Ehden by Bashir Gemayel's Lebanese Forces — one of the most consequential intra-Maronite killings of the civil war, which permanently poisoned relations between the Frangieh and Gemayel clans.

Abdul Halim Khaddam: see footnote 13. The cable's characterization of Khaddam's Damascus announcement as "nonsense" — in the voice of Tony Frangieh relaying the GOL's official position — is a notably blunt diplomatic formulation, preserved verbatim. (The cable reads "NONESENSE" — a teletype spelling error for "NONSENSE," preserved in the raw text.)

The cable's closing note that the GOL "will not give in to demands, reach any sort of formal agreement, or accept" terms as stated by Khaddam reflects a deliberately tough public stance. In fact, the crisis was resolved within days: a ceasefire held, PM Hafez withdrew his resignation, and negotiations produced the Melkart Protocol of May 17, 1973 — an agreement that, like the 1969 Cairo Agreement before it, formally governed Palestinian armed activity on Lebanese soil while falling far short of restoring Lebanese state sovereignty. The pattern documented in this cable — military confrontation followed by negotiated agreement that neither side fully honored — repeated itself until the civil war erupted in April 1975.

The cable is signed HOUGHTON — the same signatory as cable 1973BEIRUT04974 (April 30, 1973). This is likely Roderic L. Houghton, a senior U.S. Foreign Service Officer serving at the Beirut Embassy in 1973. Ambassador William Buffum was the U.S. Ambassador to Lebanon from 1970 to 1974; cables signed by a named official other than the Ambassador typically indicate the Ambassador was absent or that the Deputy Chief of Mission (DCM) or Chargé d'Affaires dispatched the cable. The NIACT IMMEDIATE designation — requiring attention regardless of the hour — confirms the urgency with which the Embassy assessed the situation.

readerNarrative.subheadline: This cable, filed at 8:08 AM on May 8, 1973 — more than two years before the civil war — documents what the standard account of Lebanon's pre-war period does not: the Lebanese Army deploying aircraft and tanks against Palestinian refugee camps in Beirut, a Prime Minister resigning in mid-crisis, and U.S. Embassy documentation of Syrian manipulation of Palestinian factions to prevent a negotiated settlement.
readerNarrative.summary: At 8:08 AM on May 8, 1973, the U.S. Embassy filed this Night Action Immediate cable — the highest available urgency level. By that point, the Lebanese Army had already deployed aircraft and tanks against Palestinian refugee camps in the southeastern suburbs of Beirut: Sabra/Chatila, Bir Hassan, and Borj el Brajne. The Prime Minister had resigned at 5:00 AM. The fighting that produced this had started the previous evening — a deliberate attempt, in the Embassy's assessment, by Palestinian factions including the PDFLP, PFLP/GC, and possibly Syria's client faction Sa'iqa, to torpedo negotiations that were moving toward an accommodation. Yasser Arafat had been in those negotiations when the fighting started and was, according to U.S. sources, trying to calm his forces by morning. A ceasefire held. The Prime Minister withdrew his resignation. An agreement was reached. But the pattern documented here — armed Palestinian factions sabotaging diplomacy, Syrian manipulation of events, Lebanese state institutions stretched to breaking — repeated itself in April 1975. That time, there was no ceasefire that held.
keyRevelations: The Lebanese Army used aircraft and tank fire against Palestinian refugee camps in Beirut in May 1973 — more than two years before the civil war. This event is largely absent from standard accounts of pre-war Lebanon.

The U.S. Embassy assessed the fighting as a deliberate attempt by specific Palestinian factions to torpedo ongoing negotiations — not a spontaneous escalation or a response to Lebanese Army provocation.

U.S. Embassy sources documented Syrian manipulation of Palestinian factions: Syria's foreign minister publicly announced more favorable terms in Damascus than had actually been agreed, while Syrian-aligned factions (PFLP/GC, Sa'iqa) led the military attack.

Arafat was in negotiations with Lebanese politicians when his own movement's hardliners opened fire — the same dynamic documented in the April 30, 1973 cable, where BSO activists acted against Arafat's wishes.

The GOL's tough public stance and refusal to accept Syrian-dictated terms is documented here in real time. The crisis ended in an agreement — the Melkart Protocol — that resolved nothing structurally and repeated the Cairo Agreement's pattern of paper compromises.

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
May 1973: Before the War

The Lebanese Civil War began on April 13, 1975. But the conditions that produced it were visible — and documented — years earlier. This cable, filed at 8:08 in the morning on May 8, 1973, is a window into one of those earlier moments: a night when Palestinian factions opened fire on Lebanese Army positions, the army responded with aircraft and tanks, a prime minister resigned before dawn, and the U.S. Embassy sent a Night Action cable to Washington.

The fighting of May 7, 1973

The fighting began around 7:00 PM on May 7. This cable describes it as a "deliberate attempt" by specific Palestinian factions to torpedo ongoing negotiations between the PLO and the Lebanese government — not a spontaneous escalation, not a response to Lebanese Army provocation. The factions the Embassy's Army sources identified as responsible were the PDFLP and the PFLP/GC, with possible PFLP and Sa'iqa involvement. All were on the harder-line end of the Palestinian spectrum. Two of them — the PFLP/GC and Sa'iqa — operated with close ties to Syrian intelligence.

The method was systematic: rockets and mortars at military installations and the airport, followed by armed vehicles driving through the city firing at police. The stated design, in the cable's words, was "to create panic and touch off a major army-fedayeen confrontation."

The Lebanese Army's response

It succeeded in touching off a confrontation, though perhaps not the one intended. The Lebanese Army responded with aircraft and tanks. By 7:00 AM on May 8, when the Embassy filed this cable, the army had already deployed this firepower against targets in and around three Palestinian refugee camps in Beirut's southeastern suburbs: Sabra/Chatila, Bir Hassan, and Borj el Brajne.

This is a fact that does not appear in the standard account of pre-war Lebanon. The Lebanese Army used aviation and armor against Palestinian camp areas in Beirut in May 1973. The conflict was contained. A ceasefire was arranged. An agreement — the Melkart Protocol — was reached nine days later. And the episode was largely absorbed into Lebanon's managed history of crises that somehow didn't become wars.

Two years later, they did.

Arafat in the negotiations

The cable's paragraph 4 contains a detail that mirrors the pattern documented in the April 30, 1973 cable from this archive: Yasser Arafat was in diplomatic meetings — with Lebanese politicians including Saeb Salam and Raymond Edde, and with Egyptian and Syrian representatives — when the fighting started. As the U.S. Embassy had assessed nine days earlier, hardliners within or adjacent to the Palestinian movement were acting in ways Arafat had not authorized and may have been unable to prevent.

By 8:00 AM on May 8, the Embassy's contact at the Lebanese Army confirmed: Arafat was trying to calm his forces.

The Syrian dimension

The cable documents something that rarely appears in standard historical accounts of May 1973: explicit U.S. Embassy awareness of Syrian manipulation. Paragraph 4 notes that Lebanon's government suspected a "Syrian hand working behind the scene" — and gives specific reasons. The Syrian Foreign Minister, Abdul Halim Khaddam, had publicly announced terms in Damascus far more favorable to the Palestinians than what had actually been agreed in Beirut negotiations. Meanwhile, the factions the Embassy identified as having initiated the fighting — PFLP/GC and Sa'iqa — were precisely those with the closest ties to Damascus.

Syria's interest in preventing a stable Lebanese-Palestinian accommodation was clear: such an accommodation would reduce Syrian leverage over both the PLO and Lebanon. The May 1973 crisis, in this cable's documentation, was not simply a Palestinian-Lebanese confrontation. It was a confrontation in which Syrian-aligned factions were working to prevent the outcome that Arafat and the Lebanese government were moving toward.

The pattern

The crisis ended the way Lebanese crises ended in those years: a ceasefire, a political adjustment, a formal agreement. Prime Minister Hafez withdrew his resignation. The Melkart Protocol of May 17, 1973 was signed — another paper framework governing Palestinian armed activity on Lebanese soil, like the Cairo Agreement before it.

But this cable documents the pattern that the Melkart Protocol did not resolve: Palestinian hardliners willing to use military force to prevent political accommodation; Syrian manipulation of events through proxy factions; a Lebanese state deploying its army against camps and then negotiating as though the army had not just used aircraft and tanks in a residential area of its own capital; a Lebanese political class managing the crisis rather than resolving its causes.

The pattern held for two more years. On April 13, 1975, it stopped holding.

cables.subject: Beirut Tense in Aftermath of April 13 Clashes Between Phalange and Palestinians
cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review, 05 July 2006 · Now UNCLASSIFIED

Summary
Situation tense and uncertain in Beirut following clashes on Sunday, April 13, between the militia of the Christian Phalange Party and Palestinians in the Ain Ramanneh suburb. Sporadic firing and explosions occurred throughout the night and early April 14 as the GOL sought to stabilize the situation with little apparent success thus far. All American citizens [AMCITS] safe to our knowledge.[1] The next major test of fragile public order will occur at 1000Z [10:00 AM Greenwich Mean Time] today, when the funeral for up to 35 Palestinians killed — figures vary from 27 upward — is scheduled to take place. The present crisis, occurring against a background of GOL weakness and division, has disturbing potential.[2]

1.
On the basis of fragmentary and frequently conflicting news accounts and rumors, the April 13 incidents which sparked the crisis were as follows: Phalangist leader Pierre Gemayel[3] and former President Camille Chamoun[4] attended mass Sunday morning at a church in Ain Ramanneh, with both Phalange militia and GOL police in the vicinity. At approximately 0800Z [8:00 AM GMT], a Volkswagen driven by a Palestinian — allegedly belonging to the PDFLP[5] — drove near the church and was asked by a policeman not to use the street on which the church was located. After an altercation — in which some accounts claim the driver was disarmed after threatening the policeman — the Volkswagen departed.

2.
Some time later — at approximately 0930Z [9:30 AM GMT] by some accounts — another vehicle carrying four armed Palestinians entered the area and sprayed bystanders with machine-gun fire, fatally wounding three members of the Phalange militia, before speeding away.[6] At approximately 1100Z [11:00 AM GMT], a bus loaded with Palestinians — affiliation as yet undetermined — approached the area, returning from ceremonies at Shatila camp[7] to Tel Zaartar camp.[8] It is possible that the presence of the bus was accidental,[9] but the Phalange opened up on the target, reportedly killing 26 of those aboard.

3.
As news of the incident spread, firing and explosions were heard in various parts of the city — Ain Ramanneh, Shiah, Furn as Shubak, Dekwani, Ghobeiri — throughout the evening and into the morning. Barricades were allegedly erected in Sinn al Fil. Approximately 15 rockets were fired from Borj al Barajneh refugee camp[10] into the largely Christian suburb of Haret Hreik, apparently with the local Phalange office as primary target.[11] A store belonging to Phalange notable Naum Abi-Rashed was blown up, and a factory near the site of the original incidents is currently burning. During the night, incidents — some unconfirmed — were reported in various parts of the city, particularly in areas in the vicinity of Phalange offices. One of the most serious incidents occurred in the area of the Starco Center,[12] and we have an eyewitness account of firing in the vicinity of the Holiday Inn,[13] several blocks from Starco. This altercation apparently began when two persons — subsequently killed by Phalange guards — opened fire on a Phalange office near Starco.

4.
As of April 14, 0900Z [9:00 AM GMT], the situation in Beirut is tense and the population appears to be bracing for further trouble, particularly as the time for the Palestinian funeral (1000Z) approaches. The anticipated gigantic gathering of mourners, stirred by the predictable Palestinian assertion that the Phalange bears entire blame for the incidents,[14] could easily set an escalation of fighting in the already unstable atmosphere in motion. We have warned Embassy personnel to restrict their movements — although no decision to close the Embassy has been taken at this time — and are providing similar advice to non-official American citizens [AMCITS] who inquire. We have likewise advised the American Community School to suspend classes at 0900Z to permit children to regain their homes before large crowds gather for the funeral procession. At the present time, sporadic shooting in various parts of town continues. The USIS Regional Service Center in Sinn al Fil reports firing generalized in the area and has closed down. We also have reports from several sources that a general fire-fight is taking place in the vicinity of Airport Circle near Phalange headquarters, although the route to the airport and the airport itself are open according to the last report. Clashes apparently erupted this morning when Palestinians marched to nearby Quarantina Hospital — where Palestinian dead were taken after yesterday's fighting — to claim bodies for the funeral.[15] We have little information regarding the situation in other parts of the country, although there are reports of a demonstration in Tripoli and the coastal road south has been cut at Sidon.

5. — Comment
Phalange relations with the fedayeen[16] have been subject to a series of ups and downs since the large-scale confrontation of 1969.[17] The Department [of State] will recall the Kahale incident of early 1970, when the Phalange ambushed a Palestinian funeral procession and the crisis which ensued.[18] The present confrontation, however, is the most serious of its kind in the last two years — the more so as Kamal Jumblatt[19] and other “progressive” spokesmen have now called for the withdrawal of two Phalange ministers from the already enfeebled Rashid Solh government.[20] The Solh cabinet has been, over the last week or more, defending its performance in the face of strong attacks in Parliament and was, until the latest developments, expected to win a vote of confidence on April 15 by 58 to 65 votes. We suspect that the debate and vote will not occur in light of the serious situation in the country. Nevertheless, it has been the combination of Jumblatt and Gemayel which has provided support for the Solh government and on which projections of the cabinet’s survivability were based. Consequently, the apparent open break between these Jumblatt and Gemayel pillars will greatly undercut the government’s ability to deal firmly and confidently with the present crisis.

6.
We believe the current crisis also acquires a greater degree of seriousness as a result of several other factors converging at this time:

A) The recent inflammation of confessional [sectarian] divisions as a result of incidents in Sidon last month;[21]

B) The likely neutralization of the army and security forces as a result of their experience in Sidon, and the possibility that they will not be directed to act decisively in the current crisis.[22] (We have an unconfirmed report that Squad 16 forces in the area of Airport Circle fighting have orders to stand aside;[23])

C) President Frangieh’s[24] convalescence in the American University Hospital from a gall bladder operation performed April 12; and

D) The likelihood that, as last night’s events demonstrate, clashes of this kind could easily degenerate into generalized hit-and-run strikes which would almost inevitably involve foreign residents of the city.

7.
The denouement of this crisis will unquestionably depend upon the resolve and good sense of the GOL and PLO leaderships and their ability to control armed elements which have now “escaped Pandora’s Box.” It will also, as in the past, probably depend on efforts of leading political leaders and Palestinians. The GOL, according to the few conversations we have had, is extremely concerned about the situation and its potential for sparking civil strife involving Palestinians. So far their efforts appear focused on containing the situation. According to radio, the GOL has just arrested 14 persons (identity unknown). Meanwhile, Arafat[25] and other PLO leaders have reportedly been lobbying [original: “inveighing”] other Arab states, directly and through local Arab ambassadors, to bring pressure on the GOL to punish Phalangist “culprits.”[26] In short, to this moment, the elements of a “Lebanese solution”[27] to the crisis are not apparent.

8.
All American citizens [AMCITS] safe to our knowledge.

GODLEY[28]

IT POSSIBLE THAT PRESENCE OF BUS WAS ACCIDENTAL, BUT PHALANGE OPENED UP ON TARGET, REPORTEDLY KILLING 26 OF THOSE ABOARD.

3. AS NEWS OF INCIDENT SPREAD, FIRING AND EXPLOSIONS WERE HEARD IN VARIOUS PARTS OF CITY (AIN RAMANNEH, SHIAH, FURN AS SHUBAK, DEKWANI, GHOBEIRI) THROUGHOUT EVENING AND INTO MORNING. BARRICADES WERE ALLEGEDLY ERECTED IN SINN AL FIL. APPROX 15 ROCKETS WERE FIRED FROM BORJ AL BARAJNEH REFUGEE CAMP INTO LARGELY CHRISTIAN SUBURB OF HARET HREIK, APPARENTLY WITH LOCAL PHALANGE OFFICE AS PRIMARY TARGET. STORE BELONGING TO PHALANGE NOTABLE, NAUM ABI-RASHED, WAS BLOWN UP AND FACTORY NEAR SITE OF ORIGINAL INCIDENTS CURRENTLY BURNING. DURING NIGHT, INCIDENTS (SOME UNCONFIRMED) WERE REPORTED IN VARIOUS PARTS OF CITY, PARTICULARLY IN AREAS IN VICINITY OF PHALANGE OFFICES. ONE OF MOST SERIOUS INCIDENTS HAPPENED IN AREA OF STARCO CENTER AND WE HAVE EYE-WITNESS ACCOUNT OF FIRING IN VICINITY OF HOLIDAY INN, SEVERAL BLOCKS FROM STARCO. THIS ALTERCATION APPARENTLY BEGAN WHEN TWO PERSONS (SUBSEQUENTLY KILLED BY PHALANGE GUARDS) OPENED FIRE ON PHALANGE OFFICE NEAR STARCO.

4. AS OF APR 14 0900Z, SITUATION IN BEIRUT IS TENSE AND POPULATION APPEARS BE BRACING FOR FURTHER TROUBLE, PARTICULARLY AS TIME FOR PALESTINIAN FUNERAL (1000Z) APPROACHES. ANTICIPATED GIGANTIC GATHERING OF MOURNERS, STIRRED BY PREDICTABLE PALESTINIAN ASSERTION THAT PHALANGE BEARS ENTIRE BLAME FOR INCIDENTS, COULD EASILY SET ESCALATION OF FIGHTING IN ALREADY UNSTABLE ATMOSPHERE IN MOTION. WE HAVE WARNED EMBASSY PERSONNEL TO RESTRICT THEIR MOVEMENTS (ALTHOUGH NO RPT NO DECISION TO CLOSE EMBASSY HAS BEEN TAKEN AT THIS TIME) AND ARE PROVIDING SIMILAR ADVICE TO NON-OFFICIAL AMCITS WHO INQUIRE. WE HAVE LIKEWISE ADVISED AMERICAN COMMUNITY SCHOOL TO SUSPEND CLASSES AT 0900Z TODAY TO PERMIT CHILDREN TO REGAIN THEIR HOMES BEFORE LARGE CROWDS GATHER FOR FUNERAL PROCESSION. AT PRESENT TIME, SPORADIC SHOOTING IN VARIOUS PARTS OF TOWN CONTINUES. USIS REGIONAL SERVICE CENTER IN SINN AL FIL REPORTS FIRING GENERALIZED IN AREA AND HAS CLOSED DOWN. WE ALSO HAVE REPORTS FROM SEVERAL SOURCES THAT GENERAL FIRE-FIGHT TAKING PLACE IN VICINITY OF AIRPORT CIRCLE NEAR PHALANGE HEADQUARTERS ALTHOUGH ROUTE TO AIRPORT AND AIRPORT ITSELF OPENED ACCORDING LAST REPORT. CLASHES APPARENTLY ERUPTED THIS MORNING WHEN PALESTINIANS MARCHED TO NEARBY QUARANTINA HOSPITAL, WHERE PALESTINIAN DEAD WERE TAKEN AFTER YESTERDAY'S FIGHTING, TO CLAIM BODIES FOR FUNERAL. WE HAVE LITTLE INFO RE SITUATION IN OTHER PARTS OF COUNTRY, ALTHOUGH THERE ARE REPORTS OF DEMONSTRATION IN TRIPOLI AND COASTAL ROAD SOUTH HAS BEEN CUT AT SIDON.

5. COMMENT: PHALANGE RELATIONS WITH FEDAYEEN HAVE BEEN SUBJECT TO SERIES OF UPS AND DOWNS SINCE LARGE-SCALE CONFRONTATION OF 1969. DEPT WILL RECALL KAHALE INCIDENT OF EARLY 1970 WHEN PHALANGE AMBUSHED PALESTINIAN FUNERAL PROCESSION AND CRISIS WHICH ENSUED. PRESENT CONFRONTATION, HOWEVER, IS MOST SERIOUS OF ITS KIND IN LAST TWO YEARS, THE MORE SO AS KAMAL JUMBLATT AND OTHER "PROGRESSIVE" SPOKESMAN HAVE NOW CALLED FOR WITHDRAWAL OF TWO PHALANGE MINISTERS FROM ALREADY ENFEEBLED RASHID SOLH GOVT. WE SUSPECT THAT DEBATE AND VOTE WILL NOT OCCUR IN LIGHT OF SERIOUS SITUATION IN COUNTRY. NEVERTHELESS, IT HAS BEEN COMBINATION OF JUMBLATT AND GEMAYEL WHICH HAS PROVIDED SUPPORT FOR SOLH GOVT AND ON WHICH PROJECTIONS OF CABINET'S SURVIVABILITY WERE BASED. CONSEQUENTLY, APPARENT OPEN BREAK BETWEEN JUMBLATT AND GEMAYEL PILLARS WILL GREATLY UNDERCUT GOVT'S ABILITY TO DEAL FIRMLY AND CONFIDENTLY WITH PRESENT CRISIS.

6. WE BELIEVE CURRENT CRISIS ALSO ACQUIRES GREATER DEGREE OF SERIOUSNESS AS RESULT OF SEVERAL OTHER FACTORS CONVERGING AT THIS TIME: A) RECENT INFLAMMATION OF CONFESSIONAL DIVISIONS AS RESULT OF INCIDENTS IN SIDON LAST MONTH; B) LIKELY NEUTRALIZATION OF ARMY AND SECURITY FORCES AS RESULT THEIR EXPERIENCE IN SIDON AND POSSIBILITY THAT THEY WILL NOT BE DIRECTED TO ACT DECISIVELY IN CURRENT CRISIS (E.G., WE HAVE UNCONFIRMED REPORT THAT SQUAD 16 FORCES IN AREA OF AIRPORT CIRCLE FIGHTING HAVE ORDERS TO STAND ASIDE); C) PRES FRANGIE'S CONVALESCENCE IN AMERICAN UNIVERSITY HOSPITAL FROM GALL BLADDER OPERATION PERFORMED APR 12; AND D) LIKELIHOOD THAT, AS LAST NIGHT'S EVENTS DEMONSTRATE, CLASHES OF THIS KIND COULD EASILY DEGENERATE INTO GENERALIZED HIT-AND-RUN STRIKES WHICH WOULD ALMOST INEVITABLY INVOLVE FOREIGN RESIDENTS OF CITY.

IT WILL ALSO AS IN PAST PROBABLY DEPEND ON EFFORTS OF LEADING POLITICAL LEADERS AND PALESTINIANS. footnotes: The original cable uses "AMCINS" — an apparent transmission error for the standard abbreviation AMCITS (American Citizens). Such errors were common in teletype cable transmission of the era and are preserved in the raw text. The meaning is unambiguous from context.

The original cable spells this word "POETNTIAL" — a typographic error for "potential," preserved verbatim in the raw cable text. Such errors are common in cables transmitted via teletype. The annotated version corrects the spelling without altering the meaning.

Pierre Gemayel (1905–1984): Founder and paramount leader of the Kataeb Party (also known as the Phalange or Kata'ib), established in 1936 and modeled in part on European nationalist movements of the period, including the Spanish Falange and the Lebanese Scout movement. By 1975, the Kataeb was the largest and best-organized Maronite Christian political and paramilitary organization in Lebanon. Gemayel's son Bashir would become the dominant Maronite military commander during the civil war, assassinated in September 1982 days after being elected President; another son, Amine, served as President 1982–1988. His presence at the Ain Ramanneh church ceremony on April 13 — alongside former President Chamoun — indicates a gathering of senior Maronite political leadership, making the subsequent Palestinian attack on that gathering politically as well as physically significant.

Camille Chamoun (1900–1987): Former President of Lebanon (1952–1958), whose presidency ended during the Lebanese Crisis of 1958, which required American military intervention (Operation Blue Bat). By 1975, Chamoun led the National Liberal Party (NLP) and commanded its own militia, known as the Tigers (Numur). A rival of Gemayel within the Maronite political sphere, Chamoun nonetheless cooperated with the Kataeb on communal defense issues. His co-presence with Gemayel at the church ceremony on April 13 underscores the event's significance as a gathering of the Maronite political establishment.

PDFLP: Popular Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine. The PDFLP broke from the PFLP (Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine) in 1969 under the leadership of Nayef Hawatmeh, advocating a more explicitly Marxist line and, unusually within the PLO, a degree of openness to eventual coexistence with Israeli Jews. Later known as the DFLP (Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine). The cable's attribution of the Volkswagen driver to the PDFLP is explicitly described as "alleged" — the Embassy does not confirm it. The significance lies in the fact that the PDFLP was a PLO constituent organization, meaning that even the initial confrontation at the church — well before the bus attack — involved an individual with armed-faction affiliation.

This paragraph, read in sequence with paragraph 1, establishes the three-stage timeline that most Western accounts of April 13 collapse into a single event or omit in part. The bus attack (paragraph 2, 1100Z) was preceded by two distinct Palestinian incidents at the same location: first, the Volkswagen confrontation with police near the church (0800Z); and second — critically — an armed attack by a vehicle carrying four Palestinians, who sprayed bystanders with machine-gun fire and fatally wounded three Phalange militiamen (0930Z). The Phalange attack on the bus occurred after Phalange members had already been killed by Palestinian gunfire that morning. This sequence is documented in this cable, filed by U.S. Embassy Beirut on April 14, 1975, and is almost entirely absent from standard scholarly and journalistic accounts of the outbreak of the Lebanese Civil War.

Shatila: Palestinian refugee camp established in 1949 on the southwestern outskirts of Beirut, housing by 1975 approximately 10,000–12,000 registered refugees — though the actual population was considerably larger due to unregistered arrivals and natural growth. The camp was administered by UNRWA (United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East) but policed in practice by PLO-affiliated armed factions. Shatila would become internationally known following the September 1982 massacre carried out by Lebanese Forces militiamen — with Israeli military forces controlling the surrounding area — in which between 800 and 3,500 Palestinian and Lebanese Shia civilians were killed over three days.

Tel Zaartar: Palestinian refugee camp in the Dekwaneh area of northeast Beirut, geographically situated within what was otherwise predominantly Christian-controlled territory. The bus passengers were returning from ceremonies at Shatila (southwest Beirut) through Ain Ramanneh to Tel Zaartar — a route that brought them through the zone where the morning's violence had already occurred. Tel Zaartar itself would be besieged by a coalition of Kataeb, NLP Tigers, and other Maronite militias from June to August 1976. Following its fall on August 12, 1976, an estimated 1,500–2,000 Palestinian civilians and fighters were killed. The camp was demolished. The mention of Tel Zaartar in this cable of April 1975 is a small, inadvertent marker: the bus's destination was a place that would itself become a massacre site sixteen months later.

The Embassy's qualifier — "it is possible that the presence of the bus was accidental" — is significant. American diplomatic observers on the ground, filing within hours of the event, acknowledged that the bus passengers — returning from a ceremony at Shatila camp to Tel Zaartar — may not have deliberately entered a conflict zone or sought a confrontation. The cable declines to characterize the bus's approach as provocation. Most subsequent accounts omit this qualifier entirely.

Borj al Barajneh: One of the largest Palestinian refugee camps in Lebanon, located in the southern suburbs of Beirut (Dahiyeh). By 1975, it housed tens of thousands of refugees and served as a base for multiple PLO-affiliated armed factions. The camp remains in existence as of this writing.

The firing of approximately 15 rockets from Borj al Barajneh refugee camp into Haret Hreik — a largely Christian residential suburb — on the evening of April 13, 1975, is one of the most consistently omitted details in standard accounts of that day's violence. Occurring the same evening as the bus attack, and representing a significant Palestinian military action against a civilian residential area, it is absent from virtually all Western journalistic and scholarly narratives of April 13, which overwhelmingly focus on the bus incident as the day's sole act of violence. The cable reports the rockets' apparent primary target as the local Phalange office — i.e., a political-military target — situated within a civilian neighborhood.

Starco Center: A commercial and office complex in downtown Beirut, near the Hamra and Bab Idriss areas. The fighting in its vicinity on the night of April 13 indicates that violence had spread from Ain Ramanneh in the southeastern suburbs to the commercial heart of the city within hours of the initial incidents.

Holiday Inn, Beirut: The recently completed (1974) Holiday Inn tower in downtown Beirut was, at the time of this cable, one of the tallest and most prominent buildings in the city. Within months, it would become a major military fortress and the focal point of the so-called "Hotel War" (September–October 1975), as Palestinian and Lebanese leftist forces battled Kataeb and Maronite militias for control of downtown Beirut's high-rise buildings. Its appearance in this cable as a site of gunfire on April 13, 1975 — barely months before it became a full-scale battleground — is historically notable.

The cable explicitly notes, as of the morning of April 14, "the predictable Palestinian assertion that Phalange bears entire blame for incidents." The Embassy is here recording in real time — and characterizing as "predictable" — the Palestinian political narrative that framed April 13 as one-sided Phalange aggression. This framing, which the cable itself contradicts through its account of the two prior Palestinian attacks (paragraphs 1–2), became and has remained the dominant narrative in Western media and scholarship.

Quarantina: A mixed working-class neighborhood near the Beirut port, housing communities of Lebanese Christians, Kurds, Armenians, and Syrian migrant workers, as well as a Palestinian squatter population. The Quarantina Hospital is mentioned here as a collection point for Palestinian dead from April 13. Nine months after this cable, in January 1976, the Quarantina neighborhood would be overrun by Kataeb and allied Maronite forces. Hundreds of its civilians were killed in what is recognized as one of the worst atrocities of the civil war's early phase — an event also largely absent from standard Western accounts.

Fedayeen (Arabic: فدائيين, "those who sacrifice themselves"): Term applied to Palestinian armed fighters, particularly those conducting guerrilla operations. In the Lebanese context of 1975, "fedayeen" typically referred to armed fighters affiliated with PLO constituent organizations — Fatah, PFLP, PDFLP, and others — operating from bases in Lebanese refugee camps and the south of the country.

"Large-scale confrontation of 1969": The Embassy is referring to the October–November 1969 armed clashes between the Lebanese Army and Palestinian armed groups, which culminated in the Cairo Agreement of November 3, 1969. That agreement, brokered under Egyptian pressure, granted the PLO the right to maintain armed forces on Lebanese territory and to conduct military operations across the border into Israel — effectively ceding Lebanese state sovereignty over its own southern territory and the Palestinian refugee camps. The Embassy is situating April 13 within a pattern of recurring Phalange-Palestinian confrontation rooted in the fundamental contradiction introduced by the Cairo Agreement.

Kahale incident (1970): In early 1970, Phalange fighters ambushed a Palestinian funeral procession in the Maronite village of Kahale in the Metn district east of Beirut, killing several mourners. The incident produced a serious political crisis. The Embassy's reference establishes that targeting of Palestinian gatherings — including funeral processions — had precedent in Phalange behavior, and that the cycle of sectarian tit-for-tat violence had a documented prior history predating April 13.

Kamal Jumblatt (1917–1977): Druze feudal chieftain of the Chouf mountain region, leader of the Progressive Socialist Party (PSP), and head of the Lebanese National Movement (LNM) — the coalition of Lebanese leftist, pan-Arab, Nasserist, and progressive parties that allied with the PLO during the civil war. Jumblatt's immediate call for the removal of Phalange ministers from the Lebanese cabinet, within hours of April 13, demonstrates the speed with which political actors converted the day's violence into political leverage. Jumblatt was assassinated in March 1977 on a road in the Chouf, almost certainly by Syrian intelligence operatives.

Rashid Solh (1926–1994): Sunni Muslim politician and Prime Minister of Lebanon from October 1974 to May 1975. His government was a weak coalition attempting to navigate Lebanon's deep sectarian divisions while managing the consequences of the armed Palestinian presence. The Solh cabinet's expected parliamentary vote of confidence on April 15 — which the Embassy correctly predicts will not occur — was already contested before April 13. The cabinet's collapse in May 1975 contributed directly to the political vacuum in which the civil war escalated through summer and autumn.

"Incidents in Sidon last month": A reference to the Sidon fishermen's uprising of February–March 1975, triggered by a conflict over fishing rights between Lebanese fishermen and the Protein Company, a fishing concern with connections to President Frangieh. The dispute escalated into confrontations between demonstrators and the Lebanese Army. Maarouf Saad, a popular Nasserist politician and member of parliament, was shot and killed on March 6, 1975 during a demonstration — likely by Lebanese Army fire. His death inflamed Palestinian and leftist opinion and hardened the confrontational dynamic between the Lebanese Army and the PLO-LNM alliance. The Sidon incidents are widely considered a direct precursor to April 13.

The Embassy's concern about the Lebanese Army's neutralization proved accurate. The army's inability — and, increasingly, its unwillingness — to intervene decisively in sectarian clashes was a central factor enabling the civil war's escalation. An institution whose officers and enlisted men were drawn from all sects, and whose senior command reflected the National Pact's confessional balance, could not easily be ordered to fire on any particular community without risking its own internal fracture. That fracture came in early 1976, when significant sections of the army mutinied and joined the Palestinian-LNM alliance.

"Squad 16": An internal security unit of the Lebanese Army. The unconfirmed report that it had been given orders to stand aside during the Airport Circle fighting — if accurate — would indicate that civilian political authority had decided not to use military force to suppress the clashes. The Embassy flags this as unconfirmed but clearly regards it as highly significant: if true, it would mean the Lebanese state had effectively abdicated its monopoly on force at the very moment the civil war began.

President Suleiman Frangieh (1910–1992): President of Lebanon 1970–1976, a Maronite from the Zgharta region of northern Lebanon with close family ties to Syria's Assad family. His hospitalization for a gall bladder operation on April 12 — the day before the April 13 crisis — meant that Lebanon's head of state was medically incapacitated during the opening hours of the civil war. Frangieh was a controversial figure: in 1957, he had participated in a massacre at a church in Miziara during a blood feud with a rival family, killing approximately 20 people. This history, widely known in Lebanon, significantly limited his moral authority to act against political violence.

Yasser Arafat (1929–2004): Chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organization and leader of Fatah, the dominant PLO faction. Arafat had been based in Beirut since the PLO's forced departure from Jordan following "Black September" (the Jordanian Army's suppression of the PLO in 1970–71). His immediate mobilization of Arab states to pressure the Lebanese government — demanding punishment of Phalange "culprits" while making no reference to the two prior Palestinian attacks that morning — is documented here in real time, within hours of the events.

The cable's use of quotation marks around "culprits" signals clear Embassy skepticism about the PLO's framing. The Embassy is recording the PLO narrative — that the Phalange alone bore blame for April 13 — without endorsing it, in a document that has itself described the prior Palestinian attacks (paragraphs 1–2) that the PLO's framing erases.

"Lebanese solution": A phrase in Lebanese political discourse referring to the country's historical mechanism for resolving crises: negotiation among confessional community leaders, political compromise, face-saving arrangements, and the deliberate avoidance of decisive or conclusive action. The Embassy's assessment that "elements of a 'Lebanese solution' to the crisis are NOT — RPT [repeat] — NOT apparent" represents a strikingly bleak judgment, filed just hours after the violence began. In retrospect, it was prescient: no Lebanese solution materialized, and the civil war would last fifteen years.

G. McMurtrie Godley (1917–1999): U.S. Ambassador to Lebanon, 1974–1976. A career Foreign Service Officer with extensive covert-operations experience, Godley had previously served as Ambassador to the Republic of the Congo (1964–1966) and Ambassador to Laos (1969–1973), where he oversaw CIA paramilitary operations and the U.S. air campaign during the Secret War — earning him the nickname "the Field Marshal." His posting to Beirut placed him at the center of one of the most consequential crises of his career. Cables signed "GODLEY" indicate the Ambassador personally reviewed and authorized the dispatch.

readerNarrative.subheadline: Filed at the highest diplomatic urgency level before noon on April 14, 1975, this cable documents three separate violent incidents at the same location on April 13. The historical literature has consistently recorded one. The U.S. Embassy’s contemporaneous account of the remaining two has not entered the standard record.
readerNarrative.summary: Three separate incidents occurred on April 13, 1975, in the Ain el-Rummaneh suburb of Beirut. The U.S. Embassy documented all three in a cable dispatched at the NIACT IMMEDIATE level — the highest available urgency designation, requiring attention regardless of the hour received — before noon the following day. The historical literature has consistently identified one of these incidents as the event that ignited Lebanon’s fifteen-year civil war. This cable contains the Embassy’s contemporaneous account of what preceded it and what followed it that same evening. Neither has been incorporated into the standard documentary record of April 13, 1975.
keyRevelations: The bus attack was the third incident recorded at that location that morning. This cable documents the sequence. The standard account begins with the third.

At 9:30 AM — ninety minutes before the bus attack — this cable records that four armed individuals arrived at the same location and opened fire, killing three people. This incident does not appear in the historical account of April 13 as it has been widely reproduced.

The same evening, the U.S. Embassy recorded approximately 15 rockets fired from a refugee camp into a nearby residential area. This event appears in this cable. It does not appear in the standard account of April 13, 1975.

The U.S. Embassy specifically noted the bus’s presence “may have been accidental” — that passengers may not have been aware of the preceding violence. This qualifier appears in the primary source. It has not been carried forward in subsequent accounts.

By the morning of April 14, this cable records, diplomatic contacts had been initiated regarding the bus attack. The cable’s own paragraphs 1 and 2 document two prior incidents that same morning that are not referenced in those contacts as the Embassy recorded them.

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
The morning of April 13, 1975

Pierre Gemayel — the founder of Lebanon’s largest Christian militia party, the Kataeb — and Camille Chamoun, a former president of Lebanon, attended mass that Sunday morning at a church in Ain el-Rummaneh, a Christian suburb of southeast Beirut. Members of Gemayel’s party militia and Lebanese government police were stationed in the area. It was, in effect, a gathering of the Maronite Christian political establishment.

8:00 AM — First incident

The Embassy’s cable records that a Volkswagen, driven by an individual the cable describes as Palestinian and reportedly affiliated with an armed organization operating in Lebanon, approached the street on which the church stood. A policeman asked the driver not to use that route. An altercation followed; some accounts reported to the Embassy stated the driver threatened the policeman and was disarmed. The vehicle then departed.

This incident — documented in paragraphs 1 of this cable, filed before noon on April 14, 1975 — does not appear in the standard historical account of April 13.

9:30 AM — Second incident

Approximately ninety minutes later, the cable records, a second vehicle arrived at the same location. The Embassy’s account states it carried four armed individuals who opened fire on bystanders, fatally wounding three, before departing. The cable cites no motive; it records what was reported.

This incident — also documented in this cable, which was on file at the State Department before noon on April 14, 1975 — does not appear in the standard historical account of April 13. The subsequent event, at 11:00 AM, does.

11:00 AM — The bus

About ninety minutes after that, a bus carrying Palestinian passengers entered Ain el-Rummaneh. The passengers were traveling from the Shatila refugee camp in southwest Beirut to the Tel Zaartar refugee camp in the northeast — a route that, on this particular Sunday morning, took them through a neighborhood where Palestinian gunmen had just killed three men ninety minutes earlier.

The U.S. Embassy specifically noted in this cable that the bus’s presence “may have been accidental” — that the passengers may not have known they were driving through a violent situation. But the Kataeb opened fire. Twenty-six people aboard were killed.

This is the event that almost every account of April 13, 1975 treats as the sole incident of the day, and as the unprovoked act that started the Lebanese Civil War.

That evening — further incidents documented in this cable

As the day continued, the Embassy recorded additional incidents. Approximately fifteen rockets were fired from the Borj al Barajneh camp toward Haret Hreik, a residential area of Beirut; the cable notes the apparent target was a party office within that neighborhood. A commercial property was destroyed. A factory near the morning’s location was burning.

These events are recorded in this cable, filed before noon on April 14, 1975. They do not appear in the standard accounts of April 13. The bus attack — also documented in this cable — does.

The night of April 13 — a city fractures

By nightfall, gunfire was reported across a dozen neighborhoods. Barricades went up. Two men opened fire on a Kataeb office near Beirut’s commercial center and were killed by guards. Fighting spread to within blocks of the Holiday Inn hotel in downtown Beirut — a building that would itself become a military fortress within months.

The Lebanese Army, the cable notes, appeared to be standing down. An unconfirmed report reaching the Embassy stated that Army units near the fighting had been ordered not to intervene.

The political response

According to this cable, PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat spent the night of April 13 in contact with Arab governments — directly and through their ambassadors in Beirut — requesting diplomatic pressure on the Lebanese government regarding the bus attack. The cable records that these contacts focused on what they described as Kataeb “culprits.”

The cable’s use of quotation marks around that word is standard Embassy practice when attributing claims without endorsing them. The cable’s own paragraphs 1 and 2 contain the Embassy’s documentation of the two incidents that preceded the event these diplomatic contacts were referencing.

Simultaneously, the cable records, Kamal Jumblatt — leader of the coalition of Lebanese leftist parties allied with the PLO — called for the removal of Kataeb ministers from the Lebanese cabinet. The cable notes this without characterizing the motive; the timing is part of the documentary record.

The ambassador’s verdict

Ambassador Godley’s cable, dispatched at the highest urgency level before noon on April 14, closes with a sentence of striking pessimism:

“To this moment, the elements of a ‘Lebanese solution’ to the crisis are not apparent.”

Lebanon had always managed its crises through negotiation among its community leaders — a system of managed compromise that kept the country’s contradictions contained. Godley was signaling, within hours of the first shots, that this system had broken down.

He was right. The war lasted fifteen years.
